claim: Skeletal muscles are composed of gigantic cells called muscle fibers, packed with force-producing myofibrils.
source: Skeletal muscles are composed of gigantic cells called muscle fibers, packed with force-producing myofibrils.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about muscle structure.

claim: Regulated activity of core members of the Hippo pathway is required to support flight muscle growth.
source: We find that regulated activity of core members of the Hippo pathway is required to support flight muscle growth.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Dlg5 and Slmap are regulators of the STRIPAK phosphatase, which negatively regulates Hippo to enable post-mitotic muscle growth.
source: Interestingly, we identify Dlg5 and Slmap as regulators of the STRIPAK phosphatase, which negatively regulates Hippo to enable post-mitotic muscle growth.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data including mass spectrometry and genetic experiments.

claim: The Hippo pathway controls timing and levels of sarcomeric gene expression during development.
source: Mechanistically, we show that the Hippo pathway controls timing and levels of sarcomeric gene expression during development and thus regulates the key components that physically mediate muscle growth.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by transcriptomics data and protein level measurements.

claim: Dlg5, STRIPAK and the Hippo pathway are conserved from Drosophila to humans.
source: Since Dlg5, STRIPAK and the Hippo pathway are conserved a similar mechanism may contribute to muscle or cardiomyocyte growth in humans.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of protein conservation and is also shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A comparing Drosophila and human proteins.

claim: Each sarcomere has a length of about 3 µm in relaxed human skeletal muscles.
source: Each sarcomere has a length of about 3 µm in relaxed human skeletal muscles (Ehler and Gautel, 2008; Llewellyn et al., 2008; Regev et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Hundreds of sarcomeres need to assemble into long chains called myofibrils in order to generate force across the entire muscle fiber.
source: Thus, hundreds of sarcomeres need to assemble into long chains called myofibrils in order to generate force across the entire muscle fiber (Lemke and Schnorrer, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Large muscle fibers contain many parallel myofibrils, which are laterally aligned to a cross-striated pattern to effectively power animal locomotion.
source: Large muscle fibers contain many parallel myofibrils, which are laterally aligned to a cross-striated pattern to effectively power animal locomotion (Gautel, 2008; Schiaffino et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Mechanical tension within myotubes triggers myofibril assembly and the transition of myotubes to early myofibers.
source: This enables the build-up of mechanical tension within myotubes, which consecutively triggers myofibril assembly and the transition of myotubes to early myofibers (Weitkunat et al., 2017; Weitkunat et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In mammalian muscle fibers, sarcomeric proteins transcriptionally switch isoforms from embryonic to neonatal and finally to adult isoforms.
source: This is particularly prominent in mammalian muscle fibers, in which sarcomeric proteins transcriptionally switch isoforms from embryonic to neonatal and finally to adult isoforms (Schiaffino, 2018; Schiaffino et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In Drosophila indirect flight muscles, transcription of sarcomeric and mitochondrial protein coding genes starts just before myofibril assembly and is then strongly boosted during myofibril maturation.
source: In Drosophila indirect flight muscles, transcription of sarcomeric and mitochondrial protein coding genes starts just before myofibril assembly and is then strongly boosted during myofibril maturation, when myofibrils grow in length and width (González-Morales et al., 2019; Shwartz et al., 2016; Spletter et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The Hippo pathway regulates the activity of the growth promoting transcriptional co-activator Yorkie (Yki, YAP and TAZ in mammals).
source: One central pathway controlling organ size during development and tumorigenesis is the Hippo pathway, which regulates the activity of the growth promoting transcriptional co-activator Yorkie (Yki, YAP and TAZ in mammals) (Pan, 2010; Zanconato et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Hippo pathway supported by citations.

claim: The core of the Hippo pathway is composed of a kinase cascade with Hippo (Hpo; Mst1 and Mst2 in mammals) phosphorylating the downstream kinase Warts (Wts; Lats1 and Lats2 in mammals).
source: The core of the pathway is composed of a kinase cascade with Hippo (Hpo; Mst1 and Mst2 in mammals) phosphorylating the downstream kinase Warts (Wts; Lats1 and Lats2 in mammals) (Udan et al., 2003; Wu et al., 2003).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Hippo pathway supported by citations.

claim: Phosphorylated Wts is active and in turn phosphorylates Yki, leading to the cytoplasmic retention of phospho-Yki by 14-3-3 proteins.
source: Phosphorylated Wts is active and in turn phosphorylates Yki (Huang et al., 2005), leading to the cytoplasmic retention of phospho-Yki by 14-3-3 proteins (Dong et al., 2007; Oh and Irvine, 2008; Ren et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Hippo pathway supported by citations.

claim: When the Hippo pathway is not active, unphosphorylated Yki enters into the nucleus, binds to the Tead protein Scalloped (Sd), and turns on transcriptional targets.
source: When the pathway is not active, unphosphorylated Yki enters into the nucleus, binds to the Tead protein Scalloped (Sd), and turns on transcriptional targets (Goulev et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Hippo pathway supported by citations.

claim: The majority of Yorkie transcriptional targets promote organ growth by suppressing apoptosis and stimulating cell growth and cell proliferation.
source: The majority of these targets promote organ growth by suppressing apoptosis and stimulating cell growth and cell proliferation (Harvey and Tapon, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the Hippo pathway supported by a citation.

claim: The scaffold protein Salvador promotes Hippo kinase activity by localising Hippo to the plasma membrane and by inhibiting the STRIPAK complex.
source: In epithelial cells, the scaffold protein Salvador promotes Hippo kinase activity by localising Hippo to the plasma membrane (Yin et al., 2013) and by inhibiting a large protein complex called the STRIPAK (Striatin-interacting phosphatase and kinase) complex (Bae et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Hippo pathway regulation supported by citations.

claim: The STRIPAK complex contains PP2A as active phosphatase, which dephosphorylates a key Hippo auto-phosphorylation site and thus inhibits Hippo activity.
source: The STRIPAK complex contains PP2A as active phosphatase, which dephosphorylates a key Hippo auto-phosphorylation site and thus inhibits Hippo activity (Ribeiro et al., 2010; Zheng et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the STRIPAK complex supported by citations.

claim: dRassf can promote the recruitment of STRIPAK to Hippo and thus inactivate Hippo.
source: dRassf can promote the recruitment of STRIPAK to Hippo and thus inactivate Hippo (Polesello et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Mechanical stretch of the epithelial cell cortex directly inhibits the Hippo pathway, likely mediated by the spectrin network at the cortex, promoting nuclear localisation of Yorkie.
source: Finally, mechanical stretch of the epithelial cell cortex was shown to directly inhibit the Hippo pathway, likely mediated by the spectrin network at the cortex, promoting nuclear localisation of Yorkie (Fletcher et al., 2018; Fletcher et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: At 24 hr APF (at 27°C) myoblast fusion is largely finished in Drosophila flight muscles.
source: At 24 hr APF (at 27°C) myoblast fusion is largely finished (Weitkunat et al., 2014), and the fibers have a length of about 270 µm and a cross-sectional area of about 1000 µm2 (Figure 1A,C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and by data shown in Figure 1A,C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: At 24 hr APF, Drosophila flight muscle fibers have a length of about 270 µm and a cross-sectional area of about 1000 µm2.
source: At 24 hr APF (at 27°C) myoblast fusion is largely finished (Weitkunat et al., 2014), and the fibers have a length of about 270 µm and a cross-sectional area of about 1000 µm2 (Figure 1A,C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A,C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Flight muscles build-up mechanical tension, compact to about 220 µm in length, while their diameter grows to about 2000 µm2, and assemble the immature myofibrils at 32 hr APF.
source: Then, flight muscles build-up mechanical tension, compact to about 220 µm in length, while their diameter grows to about 2000 µm2, and assemble the immature myofibrils at 32 hr APF (Lemke et al., 2019; Weitkunat et al., 2014; Figure 1A,C).
evidence: This is supported by citations and by data shown in Figure 1A,C.

claim: After 32 hr APF, flight muscles grow about 2.5 times in length while keeping a similar diameter until 48 hr APF.
source: After 32 hr, flight muscles grow about 2.5 times in length while keeping a similar diameter until 48 hr APF.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Flight muscles grow to about 800 µm in length while increasing in diameter to almost 4000 µm2 until 90 hr APF.
source: After 48 hr APF, they grow further to about 800 µm in length while increasing in diameter to almost 4000 µm2 until 90 hr APF, which is shortly before eclosion at 27°C (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1; Spletter et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1, and a citation.

claim: The volume of individual muscle fibers increases more than 10-fold in less than 3 days during Drosophila flight muscle development.
source: Thus, in total, the volume of the individual muscle fibers increases more than 10-fold in less than 3 days (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Muscle-specific knockdown of Dlg5 using several independent RNAi constructs results in viable but completely flightless flies.
source: Our analysis identified two genes, Dlg5 (Discs large 5, CG6509) and Slmap (Sarcolemma associated protein, CG17494), which are conserved from Drosophila to human and when knocked-down using several independent RNAi constructs result in viable but completely flightless flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Muscle-specific knockdown of Slmap using several independent RNAi constructs results in viable but completely flightless flies.
source: Our analysis identified two genes, Dlg5 (Discs large 5, CG6509) and Slmap (Sarcolemma associated protein, CG17494), which are conserved from Drosophila to human and when knocked-down using several independent RNAi constructs result in viable but completely flightless flies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Muscle-specific knockdown of Dlg5 or Slmap results in complete flight muscle atrophy in pupae at 90 hr APF.
source: Inspection of the thoraces of these animals revealed complete flight muscle atrophy in pupae at 90 hr APF (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Expression of UAS-Dlg5-GFP rescues the number of muscle fibers of Dlg5 knock-down flies to wild type.
source: Expression of a UAS-Dlg5-GFP but not a UAS-GFP-Gma (globular moesin actin binding domain fused to GFP) control construct, was able to rescue the number of muscle fibers of Dlg5 knock-down (Dlg5-IR-1) flies to wild type providing further strong evidence for the specificity of the knock-down phenotype (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: At 24 hr APF, Dlg5 and Slmap knock-down flight muscles are more than 20% longer than wild type.
source: However, the fibers are more than 20% longer than wild type and fail to compact at 32 hr APF when myofibrils normally assemble (Figure 1B,C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B,C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Dlg5 and Slmap knock-down flight muscles fail to compact at 32 hr APF when myofibrils normally assemble.
source: However, the fibers are more than 20% longer than wild type and fail to compact at 32 hr APF when myofibrils normally assemble (Figure 1B,C, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B,C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: After 32 hr APF, Dlg5 and Slmap knock-down fibers undergo complete flight muscle atrophy until 48 hr APF.
source: Interestingly, after 32 hr APF, when wild-type myofibers strongly grow in length, Dlg5 and Slmap knock-down fibers undergo complete flight muscle atrophy until 48 hr APF (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Dlg5 and Slmap proteins largely localise to membranous structures called T-tubules at 90 hr APF.
source: Detailed immunostainings revealed that both Dlg5 and Slmap proteins largely localise to membranous structures called T-tubules at 90 hr APF (Figure 2A,B), which are marked by the Dlg5-related protein Dlg1 and the membrane-binding protein Amphiphysin (Figure 2C; Razzaq et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A,B,C and a citation.

claim: Mature T-tubules are in intimate contact with the mature myofibrils at their sarcomeric A-bands.
source: The mature T-tubules are in intimate contact with the mature myofibrils at their sarcomeric A-bands (Figure 2D; Razzaq et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and a citation.

claim: At 32 hr and 48 hr APF, Dlg5 and Slmap proteins partially co-localise with Dlg1.
source: Interestingly, at 32 hr and 48 hr APF when first myofibrils and then T-tubules assemble, Dlg5 and Slmap proteins partially co-localise with Dlg1 (Figure 2A,B), however, both proteins show a more vesicular pattern compared to Dlg1 or Amphiphysin at these stages (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2A,B,C.

claim: Dlg5 interacts with Slmap in Drosophila muscle.
source: Interestingly, we not only identified Slmap as a binding partner of Dlg5 in muscle, but also Fgop2, GckIII, Striatin (Cka), and the catalytic subunit of PP2A phosphatase (Mts) (Figure 3A,B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3A,B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Dlg5 interacts with Fgop2, GckIII, Striatin (Cka), and the catalytic subunit of PP2A phosphatase (Mts) in Drosophila muscle.
source: Interestingly, we not only identified Slmap as a binding partner of Dlg5 in muscle, but also Fgop2, GckIII, Striatin (Cka), and the catalytic subunit of PP2A phosphatase (Mts) (Figure 3A,B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 3A,B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: The composition of the STRIPAK complex in fly muscles is similar to mammals.
source: All these proteins are members of the STRIPAK complex and have been described to interact closely in mammals (Hwang and Pallas, 2014). This suggests that the composition of the STRIPAK complex in fly muscles is similar to mammals (Figure 3C), and Dlg5 is either a core member or closely interacts with this complex in muscle.
evidence: This is inferred from the mass spectrometry data and comparison to mammalian literature.

claim: Knock-down of Striatin (Cka) and Strip results in flight muscle compaction defects at 32 hr APF and muscle atrophy after 32 hr APF.
source: To functionally test if members of the STRIPAK complex other than Dlg5 and Slmap play a similarly important role in flight muscles, we knocked-down various component members and found that knock-down of Striatin (Cka) and Strip indeed result in very similar phenotypes to Dlg5 and Slmap knock-down: flight muscles at 32 hr APF are longer than wild type, suggesting a fiber compaction defect, and undergo muscle atrophy after 32 hr APF (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: Knock-down of yorkie in muscles results in a failure of muscle compaction at 32 hr APF, flight muscle atrophy at 48 hr APF and flightless adults.
source: When knocking-down the Hippo pathway transcriptional co-activator yorkie in muscles, we observed a failure of muscle compaction at 32 hr APF, flight muscle atrophy at 48 hr APF and consequently flightless adults (Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Expression of an activated form of Yorkie (yorkie-CA) results in premature muscle fiber compaction already at 24 hr APF and strongly hyper-compacted muscle fibers at 32 hr APF.
source: In contrast to the myofiber compaction defect of yorkie knock-down muscles, expression of an activated form of Yorkie (yorkie-CA), which cannot be phosphorylated by Warts, results in premature muscle fiber compaction already at 24 hr APF and strongly hyper-compacted muscle fibers at 32 hr APF, and later in disorganised myofibers (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Knock-down of hippo and warts results in premature muscle fiber compaction at 24 hr APF and hyper-compacted muscle fibers at 32 hr APF.
source: Importantly, we observed the same phenotypes after knock-down of each of the two kinases hippo and warts, both negative regulators of Yorkie nuclear entry (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Dlg5, Slmap, hippo, warts, yorkie and scalloped are all expressed in developing flight muscles.
source: Consistently, a transcriptomics time-course of dissected developing flight muscles (Spletter et al., 2018) showed that Dlg5, Slmap, hippo, warts, yorkie and also the transcriptional activator scalloped are all expressed in developing flight muscles (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomics data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and a citation.

claim: Expression of hippo[4A/431T] in muscle results in a muscle fiber compaction defect at 32 hr APF and muscle atrophy thereafter.
source: Interestingly, expression of hippo[4A/431T] in muscle after Mef2-GAL4 driven flip-out also resulted in a muscle fiber compaction defect at 32 hr APF and muscle atrophy thereafter, phenocopying the STRIPAK and yorkie loss-of-function phenotypes (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Conditional activation of GAL4 only during pupal stages using temperature sensitive GAL80 does not affect myoblast fusion rates as measured by nuclei counts at 24 hr APF.
source: Hence, we conditionally activated GAL4 only during pupal stages using temperature sensitive GAL80 (GAL80ts, see Materials and methods) (McGuire et al., 2003) and quantified myoblast fusion rates by counting the nuclei of DLM4. We found comparable numbers of nuclei at 24 hr APF ruling out a major contribution of myoblast proliferation or fusion defect to the phenotype (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B and a citation.

claim: GAL80ts Mef2-GAL4 Dlg5 and yorkie knock-down muscles display the same fiber compaction defect as observed with Mef2-GAL4.
source: Importantly, these GAL80ts Mef2-GAL4 Dlg5 and yorkie knock-down muscles do display the same fiber compaction defect as observed with Mef2-GAL4 resulting in longer but thinner fibers with grossly comparable volumes at 24 hr APF (yorkie-IR is slightly smaller) (Figure 5A,B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A,B.

claim: Conditional expression of yorkie-CA during pupal stages results in premature compaction at 24 hr APF and very short fibers at 32 hr APF that grow to disorganised fibers at 90 hr APF.
source: Conversely, conditional expression of yorkie-CA during pupal stages results in premature compaction at 24 hr APF and very short fibers at 32 hr APF that grow to disorganised fibers at 90 hr APF (Figure 5A–D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5A–D.

claim: Post-mitotic over-expression of hippo with Act88F-GAL4 results in flight muscle compaction defects at 32 hr APF and muscle atrophy at 48 hr APF.
source: To further corroborate a post-mitotic role of the Hippo pathway in muscle fibers, we over-expressed hippo with the strong, strictly post-mitotic flight muscle specific driver Act88F-GAL4, which is only active after myoblast fusion (Bryantsev et al., 2012; Spletter et al., 2018). This post-mitotic over-expression of hippo resulted in flight muscle compaction defects at 32 hr APF and muscle atrophy at 48 hr APF (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 5E and citations.

claim: Over-expression of Diap1 during pupal stages in GAL80ts yorkie or Dlg5 knock-down fibers substantially rescues fiber atrophy, often resulting in the normal number of six muscle fibers at 48 hr APF.
source: Indeed, over-expression of Diap1 using UAS-Diap1 but not of a control construct (UAS-GFP-Gma) during pupal stages in GAL80ts Mef2-GAL4 (hereafter abbreviated as GAL80ts) yorkie or Dlg5 knock-down fibers substantially rescues fiber atrophy, often resulting in the normal number of six muscle fibers at 48 hr APF (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Over-expression of the exogenous apoptosis inhibitor p35 results in six muscle fibers at 48 hr APF in yorkie and Dlg5 knock-down muscles.
source: Furthermore, over-expression of the exogenous apoptosis inhibitor p35 (Clem et al., 1991) also results in six muscle fibers at 48 hr APF (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C and a citation.

claim: Apoptosis contributes to flight muscle fiber atrophy in yorkie and Dlg5 knock-down muscles.
source: This demonstrates that apoptosis contributes to flight muscle fiber atrophy in yorkie and Dlg5 knock-down muscles.
evidence: This is inferred from the rescue experiments with Diap1 and p35.

claim: GAL80ts Diap1-expressing yorkie or Dlg5 knock-down muscles fail to normally increase their cross-sectional area at 32 hr and 48 hr APF, resulting in smaller volumes at 48 hr APF.
source: Interestingly, GAL80ts Diap1-expressing yorkie or Dlg5 knock-down muscles fail to normally increase their cross-sectional area at 32 hr and 48 hr APF, thus resulting in smaller volumes at 48 hr APF (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 6A–C.

claim: The Hippo pathway and its transcriptional co-activator Yorkie are required to enable normal post-mitotic growth of flight muscle fibers.
source: Taken together, these data provide strong evidence that the Hippo pathway and its transcriptional co-activator Yorkie are required to enable normal post-mitotic growth of flight muscle fibers, likely by regulating the developmental timing of muscle morphogenesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the growth defects observed in yorkie and Dlg5 knock-down muscles even when apoptosis is inhibited.

claim: GAL80ts Diap1-expressing yorkie or Dlg5 knock-down muscles fail to properly assemble their myofibrils at 32 hr APF resulting in only short myofibril traces.
source: In contrast, GAL80ts Diap1-expressing yorkie or Dlg5 knock-down muscles fail to properly assemble their myofibrils at 32 hr APF resulting in only short myofibril traces (Figure 7A,B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7A,B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: In yorkie and Dlg5 knock-down muscles, nuclei form large centrally located clusters instead of being present mainly as single rows located between myofibril bundles.
source: Concomitant with the myofibril assembly defect, we also found that the spacing of the nuclei is defective. In control muscle fibers the nuclei are present mainly as single rows located between myofibril bundles, whereas in yorkie and Dlg5 knock-down muscles they form large centrally located clusters (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: At 48 hr APF, the total number of myofibrils is strongly reduced in GAL80ts yorkie and Dlg5 knock-down muscles compared to control.
source: Furthermore, cryo cross-sections revealed that not only the cross-sectional area but also the total number of myofibrils is strongly reduced in GAL80ts yorkie and Dlg5 knock-down muscles compared to control (Figure 7C,D, Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7C,D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The Hippo pathway controls both the morphological quality of the myofibrils at the assembly and maturation stages as well as their quantity.
source: As myofibril number is determined at the assembly stage at 32 hr APF in wild type (Spletter et al., 2018) these data demonstrate that the Hippo pathway controls both the morphological quality of the myofibrils at the assembly and maturation stages as well as their quantity.
evidence: This is inferred from the myofibril defects observed in yorkie and Dlg5 knock-down muscles and supported by a citation.

claim: Hypomorphic knock-down of the muscle attachment protein Kon-tiki (kon) results in a fiber compaction defect at 32 hr APF and a strongly reduced fiber cross-sectional area and volume at 48 hr APF.
source: Upon hypomorphic knock-down of the muscle attachment protein Kon-tiki (kon), muscle-tendon attachment is compromised, hence mechanical tension build-up is perturbed and only fewer myofibrils can assemble (Weitkunat et al., 2014). Consistent with our results after yorkie or Dlg5 knock-down we find that kon knock-down also results in a fiber compaction defect, caused by reduced mechanical tension at 32 hr APF (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D), and as a consequence in a strongly reduced fiber cross-sectional area and volume at 48 hr APF (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1D–F and a citation.

claim: Both mechanical tension and regulated Yorkie activity are required for normal myofibril morphogenesis to support muscle fiber growth.
source: Taken together, these data strongly suggest that both mechanical tension and regulated Yorkie activity are required for normal myofibril morphogenesis to support muscle fiber growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of kon knock-down and yorkie/Dlg5 knock-down phenotypes.

claim: Over-expression of either Yorkie-CA or wild-type Yorkie post-mitotically using Act88F-GAL4 results in premature muscle fiber compaction at 24 hr APF.
source: Over-expression of either Yorkie-CA, whose import into the nucleus is uncoupled from the Hippo pathway, or wild-type Yorkie, whose nuclear import is regulated by Hippo, both result in premature muscle fiber compaction at 24 hr APF, with seemingly normal actin filaments, phenocopying the Gal80ts condition (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: The muscle fiber hyper-compaction at 32 hr APF upon Yorkie over-expression coincides with a chaotic organisation of the myofibrils.
source: Strikingly, the muscle fiber hyper-compaction at 32 hr APF coincides with a chaotic organisation of the myofibrils, with many myofibrils not running in parallel but in various directions (Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7E and Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Over-expression of a membrane-anchored myristoylated form of Yorkie does not result in premature muscle fiber compaction at 24 hr APF and displays normally oriented parallel myofibrils at 32 hr APF.
source: In contrast, over-expression of a membrane-anchored myristoylated form of Yorkie, which has been shown to activate myosin contractility at the epithelial cell cortex without going into the nucleus (Xu et al., 2018), does not result in premature muscle fiber compaction at 24 hr APF. Furthermore, these muscles display normally oriented parallel myofibrils at 32 hr APF (Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7E, Figure 7—figure supplement 2A, and a citation.

claim: The observed myofibril and fiber compaction defects are caused by a transcriptional response of Yorkie in the nucleus.
source: These results indicate that the observed myofibril and fiber compaction defects are caused by a transcriptional response of Yorkie in the nucleus.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of nuclear and membrane-tethered Yorkie over-expression phenotypes.

claim: Knock-down of scalloped results in severe muscle atrophy and no remaining muscles at 90 hr APF.
source: This interpretation is corroborated by loss-of-function data of the transcriptional activator scalloped (sd), which is the essential transcriptional co-factor of Yorkie in the nucleus. Knock-down of scalloped results in severe muscle atrophy and no remaining muscles at 90 hr APF (Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Expression of many core sarcomeric components is consistently reduced in yorkie 'loss-of-function' muscle genotypes (Dlg5-IR, Slmap-IR, and yorkie-IR) at 24 hr APF.
source: Importantly, expression of many core sarcomeric components, including both titin homologs sallimus (sls) and bent (bt), Myosin heavy chain (Mhc), Myofilin (Mf), Paramyosin (Prm), tropomyosins (Tm1, Tm2), flight-muscle-specific actin (Act88F) and Obscurin (Unc-89), as well as sarcomere dynamics regulators, including myosin phosphatase (Mbs), a flight muscle formin (Fhos) and the spektraplakin shortstop (shot) are consistently reduced in yorkie 'loss-of-function' muscle genotypes at 24 hr APF (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomics data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Expression of mRNAs coding for proteins linking the nuclei to the cytoskeleton, such as the Nesprin family members klar and Msp300, are strongly reduced in yorkie 'loss-of-function' muscle genotypes at 24 hr APF.
source: Furthermore, expression of mRNAs coding for proteins linking the nuclei to the cytoskeleton, such as the Nesprin family members klar and Msp300, are also strongly reduced (Figure 8B), which may explain the observed nuclei positioning defect in yorkie and Dlg5 knock-down muscles (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomics data shown in Figure 8B and inferred to explain the nuclei positioning defect.

claim: Sarcomeric core components and their regulators are amongst the top upregulated genes in yorkie-CA and hippo-IR myofibers at 32 hr APF.
source: Strikingly, sarcomeric core components and their regulators are amongst the top upregulated genes on both lists (Figure 8B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomics data shown in Figure 8B and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Genes important for myofibril attachment at muscle-tendon junctions, including the integrin attachment complex members kon, if, CAP, by, and Kank are upregulated in both yorkie-CA and hippo-IR genotypes at 32 hr APF.
source: In addition to sarcomeric genes, genes important for myofibril attachment at muscle-tendon junctions, including the integrin attachment complex members kon, if, CAP, by, and Kank are upregulated in both gain-of-function genotypes (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomics data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: mRNAs coding for respiratory chain components are upregulated in hippo-IR and yorkie-CA myofibers at 32 hr APF.
source: Consistently, we found an induction of mitochondria dynamics and protein import regulators (Opa1, Tom40) in hippo-IR and yorkie-CA myofibers at 32 hr APF as well as a consistent upregulation of mRNAs coding for respiratory chain components, including the F1F0 ATP synthase complex (complex V) subunit blw, the NADH dehydrogenase (ubiquinone) subunit ND-75 and the Ubiquinol-cytochrome c reductase subunit UQCR-C2, which are all required to boost ATP production during muscle fiber growth (Figure 8A,B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is supported by transcriptomics data shown in Figure 8A,B and Supplementary file 2.

claim: There is a mild reduction of Mhc and Act88F protein levels in yorkie knock-down muscles at 24 hr APF, which becomes more pronounced at 32 hr APF.
source: Consistent with the transcriptomics data, we found a mild reduction of Mhc and Act88F protein levels in yorkie knock-down muscles at 24 hr APF, which became more pronounced at 32 hr APF (Figure 9A–C).
evidence: This is supported by protein level quantification data shown in Figure 9A–C.

claim: There is a reduction of Sls-GFP at 24 hr APF and a severe reduction of Prm-GFP at 32 hr APF in yorkie knock-down muscles.
source: Furthermore, we have investigated protein levels for the myosin-binding protein Paramyosin (Prm) and the titin homolog Sls also using GFP fusion proteins. We found a reduction of Sls-GFP at 24 hr APF and a severe reduction of Prm-GFP at 32 hr APF in yorkie knock-down muscles (Figure 9—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by protein level quantification data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: Constitutive activation of yorkie (yorkie-CA) results in a boost of Mhc-GFP, Act88F-GFP, Sls-GFP, and Prm-GFP protein expression already at 24 hr APF, which is maintained at 32 hr APF.
source: Surprisingly, constitutive activation of yorkie (yorkie-CA) results in a boost of Mhc-GFP, Act88F-GFP, Sls-GFP, and Prm-GFP protein expression already at 24 hr APF, which is maintained at 32 hr APF (Figure 9A–C, Figure 9—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by protein level quantification data shown in Figure 9A–C and Figure 9—figure supplement 1A–C.

claim: The increased acto-myosin and titin expression in yorkie-CA muscles may provide the molecular explanation of the premature compaction phenotype seen at 24 hr APF.
source: This increased acto-myosin and titin expression may provide the molecular explanation of the premature compaction phenotype seen in yorkie-CA muscles at 24 hr APF.
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between increased protein levels and premature compaction.

claim: The Hippo pathway and its transcriptional regulator Yorkie contribute to the timing of myofibril assembly by regulating correct timing and levels of sarcomeric protein expression.
source: Taken together, these data provide strong evidence that the Hippo pathway and its transcriptional regulator Yorkie contribute to the timing of myofibril assembly by regulating correct timing and levels of sarcomeric protein expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined transcriptomics and protein level data showing dysregulation in both loss and gain of function conditions.

claim: Mammalian YAP1 can promote cardiomyocyte survival and growth, as post-mitotic deletion of YAP1 results in increased fibrosis and cardiomyocyte apoptosis.
source: Interestingly, it was shown that mammalian YAP1 can promote cardiomyocyte survival and growth, as post-mitotic deletion of YAP1 results in increased fibrosis and cardiomyocyte apoptosis (Del Re et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge from mammalian studies supported by a citation.

claim: Constitutive expression of active YAP in adult mouse muscle fibers induces muscle fiber atrophy and deterioration of muscle function.
source: However, a role for the Hippo pathway in mammalian muscle is not limited to the heart. Constitutive expression of active YAP in adult mouse muscle fibers induces muscle fiber atrophy and deterioration of muscle function (Judson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge from mammalian studies supported by a citation.

claim: The mammalian Hippo homolog Mst1 is a key regulator in fast skeletal muscle atrophy.
source: Furthermore, it has been shown that the mammalian Hippo homolog Mst1 is a key regulator in fast skeletal muscle atrophy (Wei et al., 2013), and more importantly YAP promotes muscle fiber growth by its transcriptional activity requiring Tead cofactors (Watt et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge from mammalian studies supported by citations.

claim: YAP promotes muscle fiber growth by its transcriptional activity requiring Tead cofactors.
source: Furthermore, it has been shown that the mammalian Hippo homolog Mst1 is a key regulator in fast skeletal muscle atrophy (Wei et al., 2013), and more importantly YAP promotes muscle fiber growth by its transcriptional activity requiring Tead cofactors (Watt et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge from mammalian studies supported by a citation.

claim: The Hippo pathway via its transcriptional regulators Yorkie/YAP/TAZ is a general regulator of muscle fiber growth and survival in animals.
source: This suggests that the Hippo pathway via its transcriptional regulators Yorkie/YAP/TAZ is a general regulator of muscle fiber growth and survival in animals.
evidence: This is inferred from the conservation of the pathway and similar phenotypes in flies and mammals.

claim: Mammalian homologs Tead1-4 bind to a DNA motif called 'muscle CAT' (MCAT), a motif well-known to regulate cardiac skeletal sarcomeric protein expression.
source: Interestingly, it has been shown that mammalian homologs Tead1-4 bind to a DNA motif called 'muscle CAT' (MCAT), a motif well-known to regulate cardiac skeletal sarcomeric protein expression, including cardiac Troponin T or cardiac actin (Carson et al., 1996; Farrance and Ordahl, 1996; Farrance et al., 1992; Wackerhage et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The only Drosophila Tead family member Scalloped binds to a very similar MCAT motif.
source: The only Drosophila Tead family member Scalloped binds to a very similar MCAT motif (Wu et al., 2008), and we found loss of scalloped shows the same phenotype as loss-of-function of yorkie.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation and corroborated by the phenotypic data.

claim: Yorkie and Scalloped cooperate in Drosophila muscle to transcriptionally boost sarcomeric gene expression to enable myofibril assembly and flight muscle fiber growth.
source: This strongly suggests that Yorkie and Scalloped cooperate in Drosophila muscle to transcriptionally boost sarcomeric gene expression to enable myofibril assembly and flight muscle fiber growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the genetic and transcriptomics data showing that both Yorkie and Scalloped are required for normal muscle development.

claim: Flight muscle fate is determined by the zinc finger transcriptional regulator Spalt major.
source: It has been shown that flight muscle fate is determined by the zinc finger transcriptional regulator Spalt major (Schönbauer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Bruno is the major splice regulator of flight muscle alternative splicing of sarcomeric proteins, downstream of Spalt.
source: One interesting link is that Yorkie and the Hippo pathway are required for the normal expression of bruno1 (bru1, see Figure 8B). Bruno is the major splice regulator of flight muscle alternative splicing of sarcomeric proteins, downstream of Spalt (Spletter et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation and corroborated by the transcriptomics data.

claim: Bruno binds to 3'-UTRs of mRNA to regulate their translation efficiencies.
source: Additionally, Bruno was shown to bind to 3'-UTRs of mRNA to regulate their translation efficiencies (Webster et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Imp (IGF-II mRNA-binding protein) has been shown to regulate the stability and translation of a number of F-actin regulators.
source: Another RNA-binding protein that requires the Hippo pathway for normal expression is Imp (IGF-II mRNA-binding protein, see Figure 8B). Imp has been shown to regulate the stability and translation of a number of F-actin regulators (Medioni et al., 2014), suggesting that post-transcriptional effects of Hippo signalling can play an important role, too.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation and corroborated by the transcriptomics data.

claim: Post-transcriptional effects of Hippo signalling can play an important role in muscle development.
source: Imp has been shown to regulate the stability and translation of a number of F-actin regulators (Medioni et al., 2014), suggesting that post-transcriptional effects of Hippo signalling can play an important role, too.
evidence: This is speculated based on the regulation of RNA-binding proteins by the Hippo pathway.

claim: Crosstalk between the Hippo pathway and translational regulation via the mTORC1 complex has been suggested in mammals.
source: A similar crosstalk between the Hippo pathway and translational regulation via the mTORC1 complex has been suggested in mammals (Hansen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Salvador, Expanded, Merlin, and Kibra, which regulate activity or plasma membrane localisation of Hippo in epithelial cells, all appear not to be required in flight muscles.
source: Salvador, Expanded, Merlin, and Kibra, which regulate activity or plasma membrane localisation of Hippo in epithelial cells, all appear not to be required in flight muscles (Schnorrer et al., 2010; and data not shown).
evidence: This is based on a citation and unpublished data.

claim: Strip and Cka have been shown to bind to each other and regulate either Hippo or other signalling pathways in other Drosophila tissues including eye, testis or motor neurons.
source: Interestingly, Strip and Cka have been shown to bind to each other and regulate either Hippo or other signalling pathways in other Drosophila tissues including eye, testis or motor neurons (La Marca et al., 2019; Neal et al., 2020; Neisch et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Slmap appears to be the specific adaptor to link STRIPAK to Hippo in muscle and epithelia in flies as well as in mammalian cell culture.
source: Slmap appears to be the specific adaptor to link STRIPAK to Hippo in muscle (our work) and epithelia in flies (Neal et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2017) as well as in mammalian cell culture (Bae et al., 2017; Kwan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on the current study's data and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Slmap has a single transmembrane domain and is likely localised to vesicles.
source: As Slmap has a single transmembrane domain, it is likely localised to vesicles and our antibody stainings are consistent with at least a partial co-localisation to the assembling T-tubules, membrane invaginations that form during myofibrillogenesis and link the plasma membrane to the forming sarcomeres and the sarcoplasmic reticulum (Peterson and Krasnow, 2015; Razzaq et al., 2001; Sauerwald et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the protein structure and supported by immunostaining data and citations.

claim: Dlg5 and Slmap were found in a complex with Mst1 (Hippo homolog) in mammalian cell culture.
source: Slmap may either bind or recruit Dlg5 to membranes, both were interestingly found in a complex with Mst1 (Hippo homolog) in mammalian cell culture (Kwan et al., 2016), which may boost the interaction of STRIPAK with Hippo, resulting in its effective de-phosphorylation.
evidence: This is established knowledge from mammalian studies supported by a citation.

claim: Mechanical tension produced by the actin cytoskeleton potentially via membranes, STRIPAK and Dlg5 may inhibit Hippo and thus promote the nuclear localisation of Yorkie.
source: In analogy to the epithelial cell cortex, we hypothesise that mechanical stretch produced by the actin cytoskeleton potentially via membranes, STRIPAK and Dlg5 may inhibit Hippo and thus promote the nuclear localisation of Yorkie, which in turn will boost transcription of mRNAs coding for sarcomeric components.
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed by the authors based on their data and analogy to epithelial cells.

claim: Filamentous actin (F-actin) levels can directly regulate Hippo pathway activity; more F-actin blocks Hippo signalling, resulting in epithelial tissue over-growth.
source: Interestingly, it was shown that filamentous actin (F-actin) levels can directly regulate Hippo pathway activity; more F-actin blocks Hippo signalling, resulting in epithelial tissue over-growth (Fernández et al., 2011; Sansores-Garcia et al., 2011; Yin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A feedback loop may enable the induction of more actin and myosin once the myofibrils have started to assemble and produce high levels of mechanical tension.
source: A similar feedback loop may enable the induction of more actin and myosin once the myofibrils have started to assemble and produce high levels of mechanical tension (Figure 10).
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed by the authors based on their data.

claim: Only the successful completion of the myofibril assembly step allows to fully boost sarcomeric mRNA transcription and translation to enable myofibril maturation and muscle fiber growth.
source: This feedback model implies that only the successful completion of the myofibril assembly step then allows to fully boost sarcomeric mRNA transcription and translation to enable myofibril maturation and muscle fiber growth.
evidence: This is inferred from the proposed feedback model and the temporal separation of myofibril assembly and maturation.

claim: Mechanical control of the Hippo pathway and YAP/TAZ localisation by the actomyosin cytoskeleton is prominent in mammalian cells.
source: Mechanical control of the Hippo pathway and YAP/TAZ localisation by the actomyosin cytoskeleton is also prominent in mammalian cells (Dupont et al., 2011; Wada et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A mechanical feedback model may be a relevant mechanism to coordinate post-mitotic cardiomyocyte and skeletal muscle growth or regeneration in mammals.
source: A similar mechanical feedback model as proposed here may therefore also be a relevant mechanism to coordinate post-mitotic cardiomyocyte and skeletal muscle growth or regeneration in mammals.
evidence: This is speculation based on the conservation of the pathway and the proposed model.
